One-line verdict: cleaners of vehicles and equipment are not about giving something a quick hose-down; they clean vehicles, machinery and equipment to cleaning standards and operating procedures, use cleaning agents and high-pressure equipment correctly, check cleanliness and damage, and are accountable for cleaning quality and job safety; O*NET defines the occupation as cleaning vehicles, machinery and other equipment with water and cleaning agents and brushes and cloths and hoses and similar materials.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to repeat tasks step by step in a wet, noisy environment with chemical exposure, you wear protective equipment as required, and you stop and report when equipment behaves abnormally or the task exceeds your authority; the O*NET Work Context fields show that 95% are in an enclosed vehicle or operate enclosed equipment every day, 89% are exposed to contaminants every day, 74% wear common protective or safety equipment every day, 49% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 48% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day, and 62% work a typical 40-hour week.

Conditions that warrant pausing before heavy investment: you have not yet completed a full cleaning job on real equipment, nor checked the cleaning standards and the chemical and equipment manual requirements for the task; this occupation's job zone is Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation), the SVP range is below 6.0, and the education distribution is mainly high school or equivalent (high school 54%, below high school 24%). Opportunities depend more on hands-on ability and work discipline than on qualifications, but safety responsibility for chemicals, high-pressure equipment and confined spaces cannot be skipped, and the occupation page lists no national certification or national training programme.

Education, qualifications and authority must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation) with an SVP range below 6.0; in cleaning work, being hired for a post, an employer's internal operating procedures and on-the-job training, the statutory requirements for hazardous chemicals and special operations, and authority to operate equipment and move vehicles are four different things; the O*NET occupation page lists no national certification or national training programme, and this page does not present any training as a prerequisite for hiring or authority.

In one line: this is an occupation where steady execution of cleaning standards, correct use of chemicals and equipment, and stopping to report anomalies in time matter more to success than speed; if you are willing to repeat tasks to procedure and take responsibility for the safety of the equipment and sites you handle, it is worth serious consideration.

Vehicle and equipment cleaner work falls into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is cleaning work: rinsing objects and placing them on drying racks or drying surfaces with cloths and squeegees and air compressors, scrubbing and scraping and spraying mechanical parts and equipment and vehicles with scrapers and brushes and cleaning agents and disinfectants and acids and abrasives and vacuum cleaners and hoses, mixing cleaning solutions and abrasives to formula, and sweeping or shovelling or vacuuming up loose debris and recyclable waste. The second is equipment and material operation: starting cleaning equipment by push button, turning valves or handles to adjust the water and air and steam and abrasive pressure or flow at spray-gun nozzles, connecting hoses or lines to pumps or other equipment, turning valves or disconnecting hoses to drain water and cleaning solution and steam from machinery or tanks, monitoring the cleaning machine and stopping it or notifying a supervisor when it fails, and maintaining consumable stock and moving materials and equipment and consumables. The third is inspection and preparation for handover: checking whether parts and equipment and vehicles are clean and undamaged and conform to standards or regulations, painting and tinting and polishing and buffing and waxing vehicles or masking them to protect or restore colour and condition, cleaning interior plastic parts and fitting spoilers and side skirts or mud flaps, dismantling and refitting mechanical or equipment or vehicle parts and trim and doing lubrication and minor repair adjustments, and driving vehicles into or out of the workshop or a customer's workplace or residence.

Six recurring occupational judgements: whether the object and requirements of the job are clearly confirmed; whether cleaning agents, equipment and protection are ready; whether cleaning and equipment adjustment follow procedure; whether cleanliness and damage are properly checked; whether anomalies and equipment faults are stopped and reported; and whether the job and any anomalies leave a verifiable record.
Judgement one: is the object and requirements of the job clearly confirmed
First confirm the identity of the vehicle or equipment, the scope of work and the cleaning standard, and check the areas that must not get wet or be damaged; when in doubt, ask before starting.
Judgement two: are cleaning agents, equipment and protection ready

Check cleaning agents and mix ratios against the cleaning-solution formula and labels, and inspect hoses and spray guns and pressure settings and protective equipment, avoiding mixing incompatible chemicals.
Judgement three: do cleaning and equipment adjustment follow procedure

Complete pre-soaking and rinsing and scrubbing and spraying in order, and adjust pressure and flow per the equipment manual; do not raise pressure on your own or extend the contact time on sensitive parts.
Judgement four: are cleanliness and damage properly checked
Check cleanliness item by item against the cleaning standard and record any damage or corrosion or leakage found; redo failing areas to procedure and report damage rather than handling it yourself.
Judgement five: are anomalies and equipment faults stopped and reported

Editorial anomaly-handling note: when a cleaning machine behaves abnormally, pressure runs out of control or a leak appears, stop the affected work under the plan and report it, protecting people first; isolation, depressurising and leak handling are carried out by trained and authorised personnel, and untrained personnel are not required to approach fault handling.
Judgement six: do the job and any anomalies leave a verifiable record

Write the object of the job, quantities used, equipment parameters, inspection results, anomalies and handling into the record so that handover and review can trace back to the specific job and the responsible person.

Cleaners of vehicles and equipment clean vehicles, machinery and other equipment with water and cleaning agents and brushes and cloths and hoses and similar materials; the typical closed loop is confirming the object and site safety, mixing the cleaning solution and preparing tools and protection, cleaning to procedure and adjusting equipment, checking cleanliness and damage and redoing, preparing and handing over as needed, and leaving verifiable job and anomaly records.

paragraphs: The six directions share part of their skills with this occupation: working to procedure, using tools and equipment, inspecting appearance and condition, and safety and recording. The real differences lie in the object being cleaned or handled (dishes and linen, building interiors, sewage systems, equipment function, piping and valves), the handling responsibility carried and the qualifications required (confined space and special operations, maintenance diagnosis, valve commissioning). When choosing, it is better to first validate with one deliverable cleaning and inspection record than to compare names.

The comparison is based on the task and work activity descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 53-7061.00 page, the adjacent-occupation notes registered by this evidence route, and public occupational material for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial arrangement and does not constitute a conclusion about practice scope or interchangeable qualifications.

The four columns answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually means adding new skills and qualifications: the dishwashing and janitorial directions need deeper hygiene and chemical cleaning knowledge, the septic tank and sewer direction needs confined-space and sewage-work qualifications, the repair direction needs electrical and mechanical diagnostic training, the valve direction needs installation, commissioning and process knowledge, and the laundry and dry-cleaning direction needs fabric and washing-process knowledge. Cleaning, inspection and safety-record skills transfer, but each direction's authority and qualification system must be obtained afresh.

values: Fictional task: using a fictional cleaning operating procedure and the cleaning requirements of a fictional piece of equipment, produce a cleaning plan and complete the job and write the inspection and anomaly records.

Fictional materials: a fictional equipment manual extract (including the permitted pressure range and the parts that must not be hosed down), a fictional cleaning-agent label (including mix ratio and compatibility limits) and a fictional work-area safety briefing sheet.
Fictional condition: a fictional crew schedule (including the order of work and the handover deadline).
Fictional constraint: a fictional safety and chemicals management requirement (including protective equipment and waste-liquid disposal and anomaly reporting).
Step one: write the cleaning plan (order of work, cleaning agents and mix ratios, equipment parameter ranges, the parts to avoid hosing down and the protective equipment).

Step two: list the work steps and inspection items from the plan, and point out the two places most likely to go wrong (such as pressure setting or media compatibility) and the corresponding checking method.

Step three: write the anomaly-handling and recording template (the conditions for shutdown and isolation and reporting and resuming work), and state which matters exceed your work authority and must be referred to the team leader or a safety post.
Reference deliverables: one cleaning plan, one work and inspection checklist, and one anomaly-handling and recording template.

Assessment basis: whether the cleaning standard is clear, whether the media and parameters are compatible and verifiable, whether the parts to avoid are listed, whether the anomaly handling includes shutdown and reporting and resumption conditions, and whether matters inside and outside your authority are distinguished.
Several reasonable formulations are allowed; if you consider some information insufficient to judge, state clearly which parts are insufficient and what additional information is needed.

All materials in this exercise are fictional and must not be used for work on real equipment or vehicles; real work must be carried out by personnel with the appropriate authority and qualifications under the equipment manual, the operating procedures and local requirements.
The equipment parameters and cleaning-agent mix ratios given in the prompt are fictional values, to be used only to practise work planning and safety judgement methods.

One table: break the post requirements (education and training, cleaning and equipment operating experience, chemicals and safety knowledge, protection and recording habits, qualifications and authority) into condition, provable experience and where the evidence sits, item by item.
The forms of evidence include redacted job and inspection records, anomaly and handling records, and training and qualification records.
For items with no evidence, mark them clearly as to be supplied and give a plan for supplying them.

Review someone else's job and inspection record (using fictional or redacted material) and list whether the elements you checked are complete (cleaning standard, parameter settings, protective equipment, anomaly handling, records and trail).
Write down where you disagree or what needs to be added, and state the basis.
A one-page job summary: the object and requirements of the job, cleaning agents and parameters, inspection results and anomalies, and handling and follow-up.
A handover summary: the key handover points with the team leader and the next shift and the equipment conditions to watch.
A tool record: the cleaning, inspection and recording tools you used and what for, and how you protect on-site images and customer information.
A collaboration note: how you report and hand over to the team leader and to the equipment maintenance and safety posts, and how you leave a trail.

entries.answer: Day-to-day work centres on cleaning work and equipment operation and inspection records: rinsing objects and placing them on drying racks or drying surfaces, scrubbing and spraying mechanical parts and equipment and vehicles with scrapers and brushes and cleaning agents and abrasives, mixing cleaning solutions to formula, adjusting pressure and flow per the equipment manual, checking cleanliness and damage and polishing and waxing and lubricating and fitting trim as needed, and leaving job and anomaly records. The O*NET Work Context fields show that 95% are in an enclosed vehicle or operate enclosed equipment every day, 89% are exposed to contaminants every day, and 62% work a typical 40-hour week.
entries.question: What do cleaners of vehicles and equipment do every day?

entries.answer: Dishwashers clean dishes and cookware; janitors clean building interiors and public areas; septic tank and sewer workers handle sewage systems; repairers restore equipment function; this occupation cleans vehicles, machinery and equipment themselves and performs inspection and basic preparation. Shared skills do not mean the roles are interchangeable: the object cleaned or handled, the qualifications required and the safety responsibility differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent ones?

entries.answer: That cannot be inferred. The core tasks of this occupation include judging whether the cleaning standard is met, identifying damage and anomalies and stopping and reporting to procedure, and being accountable for the cleaning quality and safety boundaries for which the worker and the team leader are responsible; equipment and tool output can neither replace on-site confirmation nor remove the duty to work to procedure and record faithfully.
entries.question: Will AI replace cleaners of vehicles and equipment?

entries.answer: The earlier-affected stages are those that can be structured and mechanised: cleaning solution mix ratios and consumable tallies, drafts of scheduling and work orders and records, and some repeated cleaning and drying motions. The later-affected stages are those requiring on-site judgement and accountability: choosing cleaning methods and media, identifying damage and anomalies, shutdown and isolation handling, and cross-role handover and acceptance.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily automated?

entries.answer: Reading the equipment manual and the cleaning standard, judging whether media are compatible, identifying damage and anomalies and stopping and reporting to procedure, and making work and handover judgements within delegated authority that can be reviewed. These skills depend on on-site training and the constraints of operating procedures.

subject.name: Cleaners of vehicles and equipment
subject.summary: Cleaning vehicles, machinery and other equipment with water and cleaning agents and brushes and cloths and hoses and similar materials: rinsing and scrubbing and spraying mechanical parts and equipment and vehicles, mixing cleaning solutions to formula, adjusting pressure and flow per the equipment manual, checking cleanliness and damage and polishing and waxing and lubricating and fitting trim as needed, and leaving verifiable job and anomaly records.
